result:
There's a particular quality to the first sentence of anything—the way it has to stand alone for a moment before the second sentence arrives to keep it company. I've always thought beginnings were a kind of small violence, a cut into silence that can never be undone once made. You can revise a sentence a hundred times but you can't unwrite that first mark on the page, the way you can't un-ring a bell or un-meet someone. There's always a before and after now.

I'm thinking about doors today, for no good reason. The way a door is both an opening and a closing depending on which side of it you're standing on. My grandmother used to say that every door you walk through closes a hundred doors behind you, all the rooms you didn't choose, all the hallways that branch off into lives you'll never live. I found this terrifying as a child and now find it almost comforting, the way certain frightening ideas soften with repetition, like a stone smoothed by water. The same fact, worn down by years of handling, becomes something you can hold without cutting yourself.

There's a word in Portuguese, saudade, that doesn't translate cleanly into English—a kind of melancholic longing for something, sometimes something that never existed at all. I think about this word more than is probably healthy. We don't have an equivalent and so we borrow, or we describe around the edges of it with sentences like this one, circling the feeling without ever landing on it directly. Language is full of these gaps, these places where a culture decided something needed a name and another culture didn't, or hadn't yet, or had a different word that almost fit but not quite, like a key that turns partway in a lock before catching on something unseen.

I keep returning to the idea of texture lately—not just in fabric or food but in time itself. Some afternoons have a grain to them, a roughness, and others slide past smooth as glass and you can't get any purchase on them afterward when you try to remember what happened. I think this is why certain ordinary Tuesdays stay with you for decades while entire years dissolve into a kind of beige nothing. The mind doesn't archive chronologically. It archives by texture, by the catch and pull of an experience against the surface of attention.

Attention itself seems like the real currency of a life, more than time, which is really just attention's container. You can have eighty years and spend all of them with your attention scattered like seed thrown into wind, landing nowhere, growing nothing. Or you can have far less time and somehow manage to attend so fully to each moment that the moments themselves seem to multiply, the way a single candle in a dark room seems to throw far more light than its actual lumens would suggest, simply because there's nothing else competing with it.

I wonder sometimes if this is what people mean by presence, this competition-free attending. Not mindfulness exactly, which has become a word so worn from use it's lost most of its original shape, like a coin rubbed smooth from passing through too many hands. Just the simple, difficult act of being where you are instead of running some simulation of where you were or where you're going. The mind resists this constantly. It wants to be anywhere except here, doing anything except this. There's an animal restlessness to consciousness that predates all our philosophy about it.

The sky outside has gone the color of a bruise just starting to heal, that yellow-purple transition zone, and I notice I almost missed it because I was thinking about thinking instead of looking at anything. This seems to happen constantly—the meta-experience crowding out the experience, like a commentator's voice drowning out the game itself. I wonder if writing makes this worse, this habit of narrating instead of living, turning every sunset into potential material instead of just a sunset. Maybe that's an old worry though, maybe writers have always fretted about this and the fretting itself becomes part of what they write about, an endless recursive loop of noticing the noticing.

There's comfort in repetition though, in rituals small and large. The way certain phrases get worn into grooves through families, the inside jokes that don't even need the joke explained anymore, just a phrase, a look, and everyone laughing at the shape of a memory rather than its content. I think this is part of what love is, actually—not the grand gestures but the accumulated weight of ten thousand small repetitions, the same coffee order, the same side of the bed, the same way of folding a letter before sending it. Love as habit isn't the death of romance people fear it is. It might be its only real proof, the only evidence that something has survived contact with actual time instead of just the idea of time, the fantasy version where everything stays urgent and new forever.

I don't know where this is going, which feels appropriate somehow, since most days don't know where they're going either, despite our calendars and to-do lists insisting otherwise. There's something almost defiant in writing without destination, in following a thought the way you might follow a path through woods you don't know, not to get anywhere specific but because the walking itself is the point, the noticing of bark and light and the occasional startled bird is the point, and arrival, if it comes at all, is almost beside the point, a kind of afterthought to the real business of moving through time with your eyes open, paying the only kind of attention that actually counts, which is the attention you give without expecting anything back from it.
